articles.title: AI Alignment for Digital Democracy: Fairer Voters Representation against LLM Biases
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI representation is emerging in digital democracy, assisting in voter emulation and decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) behave differently depending on the model, the prompt context, and the voter information they receive, representing some groups more accurately than others and potentially making the emulation unfair to certain groups. articles.title: Economic Corridor Detection from Multi-Source Earth Observation and Commercial Geospatial Data Across Nigeria's Kilometre-Scale Grid
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31675v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Identifying economic corridors at national scale is challenging where firm registries, transaction flows, and local economic-output statistics are incomplete or unavailable. This paper develops a reproducible multi-proxy screening framework for detecting economic-corridor candidates across Nigeria using a kilometre-scale analytical grid. articles.title: Mining Frames: Association Rule Mining as an Unsupervised Framework for News Framing Detection
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31874v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computational framing analysis is dominated by supervised classifiers that require large annotated corpora and predefined frame taxonomies, limiting their use for non-English languages, novel events, and low-resource settings. This paper presents Association Rule Mining (ARM) as an unsupervised, annotation-free framework for news framing detection. articles.title: Forging Emotions: a deep learning experiment on emotions and art
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32163v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Affective computing is an interdisciplinary field that studies computational methods that relate to or influence emotion. These methods have been applied to interactive media artworks, but they have focused on affect detection rather than affect generation. For affect generation, computationally creative methods need to be explored that have recently been driven by the use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), a deep learning method. articles.title: The Effects of Generative AI on Collaboration and Social Networks Among Knowledge Workers
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32461v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence has raised concerns that knowledge work may become less dependent on human-to-human interaction. Yet because AI-generated outputs require interpretation, verification, and social legitimation, generative AI may instead increase collaboration among workers. articles.title: Analysing Austrian Parliamentary Speeches by Predicting Party Affiliations
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32515v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper examines speech characteristics of the Austrian National Council members (CMs). We introduce analysis methodology based on a fine-tuned BERT-Model which assigns to every speech a probability distribution over Austrian parties. articles.title: The Language of Instruction: Genre and Generative AI
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32982v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article argues that instruction-fine-tuned language models should be understood as implementing a genre, what is proposed as the instructional-conversational genre. This genre is an amalgamation of discursive language from prior conversations between generative models and humans recursively run through these massive neural networks. articles.title: Equity Bias: An Ethical Framework for AI Design
articles.summary: arXiv:2604.21907v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Equity Bias is a philosophical and practical framework for building more equitable AI systems. It treats AI as an interpretive agent that constructs meaning and knowledge rather than as a neutral calculator. Grounded in Gadamerian hermeneutics and epistemic injustice theory, Equity Bias views bias not as an error to eliminate but as a reflection of whose knowledge is encoded into systems. articles.summary: arXiv:2510.17753v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As human-AI interactions increasingly reshape social and research landscapes, the risks of overreliance, cognitive offloading, and the nuanced degradation of human agency have become more apparent.
